title: Values & type inference
lesson: JavaScript runs your program; TypeScript checks it before it runs. Use string, number and boolean for ordinary values. TypeScript often infers a type from an initial value. An annotation documents a boundary, such as a function parameter. Types are erased at runtime, so they do not validate incoming data.
task: Implement formatStudent(name, age). Trim the name and return "Name (age)". Give both parameters and the return value explicit types.
solution: function formatStudent(name: string, age: number): string { return `${name.trim()} (${age})`; }
hint: Use name.trim() and a template literal.

title: Functions & optional values
lesson: Function parameter and return types describe a contract. An optional parameter may be undefined. Use ?? for a fallback only when the value is null or undefined; unlike ||, it preserves an empty string or zero. Default parameters apply when an argument is omitted or undefined.
task: Implement appointmentLabel(student, counselor?). Return "student with counselor". Use "Unassigned" only when counselor is omitted. Preserve an empty counselor string.
solution: function appointmentLabel(student: string, counselor?: string): string { return `${student} with ${counselor ?? "Unassigned"}`; }
contract: const check: (s: string, c?: string) => string = appointmentLabel;

title: Objects & interfaces
lesson: An interface describes the shape of an object. Optional properties use ?. readonly prevents reassignment through that typed reference at compile time; it does not freeze the object at runtime. TypeScript is structurally typed: compatible shapes can be assigned without sharing a class.
task: Define Student with readonly id: string, name: string and optional grade: number. Implement studentSummary: "name · Grade n", or "name · Ungraded" when grade is missing.
solution:
interface Student { readonly id: string; name: string; grade?: number; }
function studentSummary(student: Student): string { return `${student.name} · ${student.grade === undefined ? "Ungraded" : `Grade ${student.grade}`}`; }
hint: Check grade === undefined rather than its truthiness.

title: Arrays & immutable updates
lesson: Use T[] or Array<T> for an array. readonly T[] accepts a read-only array and prevents mutating operations through that parameter. map transforms values; filter selects values. Return a new array when you need an immutable update. This is useful for frontend state.
example:
const names: string[] = ["Ana", "Leo"];
const labels = names.map(name => name.toUpperCase());
task: Implement activeStudentNames. Return names of active students in input order, without changing the input.
solution:
interface Learner { name: string; active: boolean; }
function activeStudentNames(students: readonly Learner[]): string[] { return students.filter(s => s.active).map(s => s.name); }
contract: const check: (s: readonly Learner[]) => string[] = activeStudentNames;

title: Unions & narrowing
lesson: A union allows one of several types. Narrow it before accessing type-specific properties. typeof narrows primitives. A discriminated union uses a shared literal property to tell object variants apart. This keeps loading, success and failure states explicit.
task: Implement normalizeId for string | number. Trim strings, and convert numbers to strings.
solution: function normalizeId(id: string | number): string { return typeof id === "string" ? id.trim() : String(id); }
hint: Check typeof id === "string" before calling trim().

title: Unknown & runtime validation
lesson: unknown means you must establish what a value is before using it. any disables meaningful checking and can hide mistakes. API responses need runtime validation even when you have TypeScript interfaces. Guard null before inspecting object properties. A type assertion alone does not validate data.
task: Implement isSchool(value): a type guard for an object with string id and non-empty string name. Reject null, arrays, numbers and blank names.
hint: Narrow object and null first, then inspect its properties.
contract: const check: (v: unknown) => v is School = isSchool;

title: Generics & reusable functions
lesson: A generic type parameter preserves the relationship between input and output types. A constraint such as T extends { id: string } states the minimum shape required. This lets you reuse one function without losing the caller’s specific fields. Prefer inference when callers do not need explicit type arguments.
task: Implement findById<T extends {id: string}>. Return the matching item or undefined. Preserve its original type.
solution: function findById<T extends { id: string }>(items: readonly T[], id: string): T | undefined { return items.find(item => item.id === id); }
hint: Use items.find(). The constraint allows item.id.

title: Utility types & keyof
lesson: Pick selects properties. Omit removes them. Partial makes properties optional. Readonly prevents assignment through the typed reference. keyof produces a union of property keys. These utilities derive types from a source shape, so changes remain consistent across your app. They do not change runtime values.
example:
interface Profile { id: string; name: string; email: string; }
type ProfileUpdate = Partial<Omit<Profile, "id">>;
task: Implement getField<T, K extends keyof T>(object, key): T[K]. Invalid keys must be rejected by the compiler.
solution: function getField<T, K extends keyof T>(object: T, key: K): T[K] { return object[key]; }
hint: Return object[key]. K determines the return type.

title: Async functions & API results
lesson: An async function returns a Promise. await unwraps the fulfilled value; rejected promises still need error handling. Model success and failure explicitly with a discriminated union. fetch does not reject merely because an HTTP response is 404 or 500: check response.ok. Validate untrusted JSON before treating it as your domain type.
task: Implement loadName(loader). Await a Promise<string>, trim the value and return a Result<string>. On any rejection return {ok:false,error:"Could not load"}.
solution:
type Result<T> = { ok: true; data: T } | { ok: false; error: string };
async function loadName(loader: () => Promise<string>): Promise<Result<string>> { try { return {ok:true,data:(await loader()).trim()}; } catch { return {ok:false,error:"Could not load"}; } }
tests: JSON.stringify(await loadName(async()=>{throw new Error("offline")})) === JSON.stringify({ok:false,error:"Could not load"})

title: Modules & project boundaries
lesson: Use export to expose a value or type and import to consume it. import type makes type-only intent explicit. Enable strict in tsconfig.json and run tsc --noEmit for checks. Keep domain types separate from presentation and API parsing. A TypeScript permission check is useful UI logic, but your backend must independently authorize access.
task: Implement exported canViewCase(user, caseSchoolId). Permit only a counselor from the same school; reject students, admins and other schools. Export the User interface too. This exercise is a single module.
solution:
export interface User { schoolId: string; role: "counselor" | "student" | "admin"; }
export function canViewCase(user: User, caseSchoolId: string): boolean { return user.schoolId === caseSchoolId && user.role === "counselor"; }
hint: Check both school equality and role. Export both declarations.
contract: const check: (u: User, s: string) => boolean = canViewCase;

title: Final project: appointment service
lesson: Combine domain interfaces, literal unions, immutable arrays and explicit result states. Separate validation from updates. Think about edge cases before implementation: incorrect school, duplicate IDs and empty lists. These in-memory checks demonstrate TypeScript skills; a real product also needs backend authorization, database constraints and transaction handling.
example:
type BookingResult = { ok: true; appointments: Appointment[] }
  | { ok: false; error: "wrong-school" | "duplicate" };
task: Implement bookAppointment(existing, incoming, schoolId). First reject a mismatched incoming.schoolId with wrong-school. Then reject an existing appointment with the same schoolId and id with duplicate. Otherwise return a new array containing incoming. Never mutate existing.
tests: Same id in other school allowed
hint: Use some() for duplicate detection and [...existing, incoming] to create a new array.
